intro: Some of the most famous secret society documents in the world were never secret and never real. A satire about a French emperor was rewritten into a hate forgery. Typed pages were slipped into a national library to invent a medieval order. An anonymous roll of film offered a top secret committee no agency had ever formed. A British television spoof about a plan to leave Earth was later repeated as a real exposé.

These fakes matter because people believed them, and some did great harm. The Protocols of the Elders of Zion was used to spread hatred of Jews for decades and was promoted by the Nazi state. In this unit you will put the people who were harmed, and the people who exposed the lies, at the center of the story.

You will also learn the historian's tools. You will compare texts in parallel columns, trace claims back to their origin, and test documents by provenance, material, anachronism and who gains. You will study one real find, the Chinon Parchment, to see that a surprising document can be genuine. By the end, you will be able to test a document yourself and explain your verdict with evidence.
bigQuestion: How do we prove a document is forged or genuine, and why do some proven fakes keep spreading?

timeline.t: Cardinals at Chinon question and absolve the Templar leaders; the record is later misfiled
Maurice Joly publishes his satire on Napoleon III in Brussels
The Protocols forgery is first printed in a St. Petersburg newspaper
Henry Ford's Dearborn Independent begins spreading the Protocols
Philip Graves shows in The Times that the Protocols copies Joly
Ford signs a public apology after the Sapiro libel suit
A court in Bern rules that the Protocols are forgeries
The Dossiers Secrets are planted in France's national library
Anglia Television airs the spoof Alternative 3
The MJ-12 papers arrive as anonymous film
Air Force investigators tell the FBI no MJ-12 committee ever existed
Barbara Frale identifies the genuine Chinon Parchment in the Vatican archives

words.d: a document made to look like something it is not, in order to deceive
writing that uses humor, irony or exaggeration to criticize real people or real power
two texts printed side by side so readers can compare them line by line
proof that one text was built from another, shown by shared wording, images and order
something placed in a time where it does not belong
the known history of a document: where it came from and who has held it
the process of checking whether a document is genuine
information spread on purpose to shape beliefs, often by misleading people
hatred of, or prejudice against, Jewish people
a trick meant to make people believe something false
when content is removed from the setting that explained it and read by a new audience without clues
when many sources seem to agree but all rest on the same original claim

test.q: Which book did the Protocols copy most heavily?
choices: The Holy Blood and the Holy Grail
test.why: Graves showed in 1921 that long parts of the Protocols copy Joly's Dialogue in Hell.

test.q: What did Joly's satire say about Jews?
choices: It blamed them for France's problems
It described a secret Jewish meeting
test.why: Joly's satire was about Napoleon III and does not mention Jews at all.

test.q: Where was Philip Graves working when he was handed Joly's book?
test.why: Graves was The Times correspondent in Constantinople in 1921.

choices: Proof that one text was built from another, shown by shared wording, images and order
A reader's need for a dictionary
A code used by secret societies
test.why: Shared wording, images and order in the same sequence show that the newer text depends on the older.

test.q: Which is still debated about the Protocols?
test.why: Historians agree it is a forgery copied from Joly, but they still debate who the forger was.

test.q: What did the Bern court find on 14 May 1935?
test.why: Judge Walter Meyer found the Protocols to be forgeries and trashy literature.

test.q: Why did Henry Ford's support make the Protocols more dangerous in America?
choices: He had proven it true in court
His fame lent the forgery credibility it had not earned
test.why: Readers trusted Ford because of his success, which had nothing to do with the text's truth.

test.q: Which statement about Ford's 1927 apology is accurate?
choices: It stopped every copy of The International Jew
Ford later took it back in court
It was drafted by Louis Marshall and signed by Ford after the Sapiro mistrial
test.why: Louis Marshall drafted it, and Ford signed it on 30 June 1927 after the Sapiro trial ended in a mistrial.

test.q: What gave the Dossiers Secrets a false look of authority?
choices: A call number in France's national library
test.why: Being deposited in the Bibliothèque nationale made the pages look official, though the library does not certify contents.

test.q: How did the MJ-12 papers first appear?
choices: As undeveloped film mailed anonymously in 1984
test.why: Jaime Shandera received the film in December 1984 with no return address.

test.q: Which of these is the strongest test result against MJ-12?
choices: Air Force investigators said no such committee was ever formed
They were published in two countries
test.why: The office that would have created the committee said it never existed, as the FBI file records.

test.q: Why did many viewers miss that Alternative 3 was a spoof?
choices: Its April Fools' Day broadcast was delayed to June, removing a key clue
It was aired only in French
The government said it was true
test.why: A labor dispute moved it from 1 April to 20 June 1977, so the April Fools' context was lost.

test.q: A reader finds ten books about the Priory of Sion, and all trace back to the 1967 papers. What is this called?
test.why: Many sources that all rest on one original claim are an example of circular sourcing.

test.q: How does the Chinon Parchment show that a surprising document can be real?
choices: It passes the tests: long provenance in the Vatican archive, medieval parchment, and fit with other records
It was found in a national library in 1967
test.why: Unlike the planted papers, the parchment passes provenance, material and consistency tests.

test.q: A post shares a passage from the Protocols but says it is about the Illuminati. What should a careful reader conclude?
choices: It is now a new and genuine document
It is harmless because no group is named
It must be true because it keeps being reprinted
It is still the same forgery, with its origin in Joly and its history of harm unchanged
test.why: Renaming the villain does not change where the text came from or what it was made to do.

write.prompt: Choose two documents from this unit, one proven false and one genuine. Which historian's test did the most to decide each case, and why? Cite at least two specific facts or sources from the unit to support your claim.
tips: Name each document, its date and where it first appeared.
Use the unit's terms: provenance, anachronism, authentication, textual dependence.
Give the strongest case on the other side before you answer it.
When you write about the Protocols, describe the evidence of copying; do not repeat its hateful claims.
End with one sentence on what your chosen test can and cannot prove.
